title: Striking hardened tools: chisels, punches, wedges and sockets
summary: Hammered tools fail by throwing steel: mushroomed heads shatter, hardened faces chip when they meet, and chrome sockets burst on impact guns. Dress or retire damaged tools, match the hammer to the job, and wear eye protection every blow.

steps.text: Put on safety glasses or goggles before the first blow (Estwing and Council Tool say goggles), and give anyone nearby goggles too. Stand between them and the chips, or put up a screen (CCOHS eyes, CCOHS struck, SafetyWorks, Estwing safety).
Look at the struck end of every chisel, punch, drift and wedge. If it is mushroomed, chipped or cracked, don't hit it (CCOHS struck, OSHA 3080).
steps.warn: A mushroomed head can shatter on impact and send sharp fragments at you or anyone near (OSHA 3080).

steps.text: Dress a mushroomed head: clamp the tool, grind or file the overhanging lip off until the end is back to its original shape, with light pressure, dipping it in cold water often (CCOHS struck; Gray punches says a mushroomed head must be dressed).
steps.warn: Heat draws the temper (CCOHS struck). On a bench grinder keep the guard on, set the rest within 3 mm (1/8 in) of the wheel and wear a face shield over your glasses (CCOHS bench grinders, CCOHS struck; see the flying fragments card).

steps.text: Throw out struck tools that are bent, cracked or chipped, and any with a slanted or damaged point (CCOHS struck).

Pick a hammer whose face is a little bigger than the struck end: about 10 mm (3/8 in) larger (Estwing safety; Gray Tools says never more than 3/8 in), though CCOHS says about 12 mm (1/2 in). Use a drilling (club) hammer or a soft-faced hammer, never a nail hammer (CCOHS hammers, Gray punches, Estwing safety).

Hold a chisel or punch in a holder or tongs, or between thumb and fingers rather than in a fist. Never let anyone hold a tool for you to strike, and don't use locking pliers as a holder (CCOHS struck, SafetyWorks, Gray punches).
Warm your hands before chiseling in the cold: don't grip a chisel with numb hands (SafetyWorks).
Strike squarely, with the hammer face flat to the struck end; avoid glancing blows (CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety).

Strike only tools made to be struck, on their struck end. Never a hammer on another hammer or on hard metal, no maul on a maul, no axe used as a wedge, no sledge on an axe (CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety, SafetyWorks, Council care, Council right tool, Gränsfors care).
steps.warn: Misuse chips hammer faces, and a chipped face is scrap (CCOHS hammers).

steps.text: Drive a splitting wedge with a sledge whose face is bigger than the wedge's head; use a maul's poll only if its maker rates it for wedges (Council right tool, Gränsfors care).
Don't strike a pry bar with a nail hammer: if a bar must be struck, use a large hammer such as a drilling hammer (Council right tool).
On an impact wrench, or an impact driver with a socket adapter, use impact sockets only, held on with the retaining pin and ring (Wright sockets, CP sockets).
steps.warn: Chrome hand sockets can crack or burst on an impact gun (Wright sockets, CP sockets).

steps.text: Don't strike steel on steel where there is fuel vapour or gas: iron and steel tools can throw sparks (OSHA 3080).

notes:
## What goes wrong
Struck tools are the ones you hit with a hammer: cold chisels, punches, drift pins, nail sets, star drills and splitting wedges (CCOHS struck). The injuries come from steel that breaks off: a mushroomed head that shatters, a chisel used as a screwdriver whose tip snaps and flies, or a hammer face that chips (OSHA 3080, CCOHS hammers). Check found tools first with [Checking a found hammer, axe, maul or sledge](#guides/test_striking_tools); the [flying fragments](#browse/hazards/projectile) card covers grinders and wheels.

## Mushroomed heads
Every blow spreads the struck end until it curls over into a thin lip, and thin edges break off when struck (Ax Manual ch13), as sharp fragments (OSHA 3080). OSHA says chisels, wedges and drift pins must be kept free of mushroomed heads (OSHA 3080).
- **Dress it early.** Grind or file the lip off and bring the end back to its original shape (CCOHS struck, Gray punches). Light pressure, and cool it in water often: heat draws the temper (CCOHS struck).
- **Grinder setup.** Guard on, rest close, face shield over your glasses ([flying fragments](#browse/hazards/projectile), CCOHS struck).
- **Retire it** if it is bent, cracked or chipped, or the point is slanted or damaged (CCOHS struck). Council Tool is stricter for mauls and splitting wedges: discard one that shows dents, cracks, chips, mushrooming or excessive wear (Council right tool).
- **Hammers are different.** CCOHS says a hammer with a mushroomed or chipped face is discarded, not ground, welded or re-hardened (CCOHS hammers).

## Two hardened faces
Chisels, punches and wedges are made to be struck, on their struck end, with the right hammer (CCOHS struck, Estwing safety). Other hard steel isn't.
- No hammer on another hammer, and no hammer on hard metal objects, stones or concrete (CCOHS hammers, SafetyWorks, Estwing safety). Council Tool's one-line version is "don't strike a hardened tool with another hardened tool" (Council care). It can't cover chisels, punches, drifts and wedges, which are made to be hit: Estwing says drilling hammers are for striking chisels, punches, star drills and hardened nails (Estwing safety).
- A nail hammer never strikes another tool; use a drilling hammer or a soft-faced hammer (Estwing safety).
- No maul driven by another maul, and no maul on concrete or metal (Council right tool).
- No axe used as a wedge or a sledge, and no hammer or sledge on an axe (Council care, Gränsfors care). Hammering on or with an axe can deform or break its eye (Gränsfors care). The poll of an ordinary single-bit axe is not hardened and mushrooms on steel wedges (Ax Manual ch13). Gränsfors rates only its splitting maul's poll for driving a wedge (Gränsfors care).
- Splitting wedges: start a notch with the maul or axe, set the wedge, then drive it with a sledge whose face is bigger than the wedge's head (Council right tool).
- Pry bars are for prying, not striking. If a bar must be struck, use a big hammer, such as a drilling or engineer's hammer; a nail hammer's face is too small and chips (Council right tool).
- Don't use a chisel as a screwdriver or a file as a pry bar: both are hard and snap (OSHA 3080, Ax Manual ch7). Cold chisels aren't for stone or concrete (CCOHS struck), and the work must not be harder than the chisel (Gray punches).

## The right hammer and grip
| Job | Hammer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Chisels, punches, star drills | Drilling (club) hammer, face about 10 mm (3/8 in) bigger than the struck end (Gray: never more than 3/8 in; CCOHS: about 12 mm) | CCOHS hammers, Gray punches, Estwing safety |
| Splitting wedges | Sledge with a face bigger than the wedge's head | Council right tool |
| Nails | Nail hammer, and nothing else | Estwing safety |

Grip the hammer near the end of the handle (SafetyWorks). Hold a chisel between thumb and fingers rather than in a fist, or use a holder or tongs; a sponge-rubber hand guard on the shaft helps (SafetyWorks, CCOHS struck). Gray Tools warns against locking pliers as a holder: they leave sharp dents that cut hands (Gray punches). Nobody holds a tool for someone else to hit (CCOHS struck, SafetyWorks). In a cold shed, warm up first: SafetyWorks says not to grip a chisel with numb hands (SafetyWorks).

## Impact guns and sockets
Hand sockets are thin-walled chrome vanadium, usually shiny; impact sockets have thick walls, a matt black finish and a cross hole in the drive end for a retaining pin and ring (CP sockets). On an impact wrench a hand socket can crack and burst, injuring the person using it (CP sockets, Wright sockets). Use impact-rated sockets only, keep the pin or ring in (Wright recommends retaining rings with air tools), and wear goggles (Wright sockets). Hand sockets stay on hand ratchets.

## Sparks
Steel striking steel throws sparks. Near fuel vapour, gas or a leaking cylinder, OSHA calls for spark-resistant non-ferrous tools (OSHA 3080). Without them, don't strike at all there: see [Gas at a damaged house](#guides/safety_natural_gas) and [Hot work on drums, tanks and cylinders](#guides/safety_hot_work_containers).

## Eye protection
In Canada, CSA Z94.3 covers eye protection. For hammering and chipping, CCOHS lists Class 1A safety spectacles or Class 2A or 2B goggles, and a face shield goes over glasses or goggles, never instead of them (CCOHS eyes, CCOHS struck). Look for the certification mark on the lens and frame (CCOHS eyes). Bystanders need goggles too (Estwing safety).

## The standards
ASME B107.400 sets performance and safety requirements for striking tools: hammers, hatchets and axes, ball-peen hammers and heavy striking tools (ASME B107.400). B107.410 does the same for struck tools (splitting wedges, chisels, punches, drift pins, nail sets, star drills, pry bars and striking wrenches), with test methods and limits of safe use (ASME B107.410). The full texts are sold, not free; this card works from CCOHS, OSHA and the makers' published warnings.

## When no help is coming
### Steel in the eye
- Don't rub or press on the eye (CRC First Aid, MedlinePlus eye).
- A loose speck: blink several times, then flush gently with clean running water (CRC First Aid). A speck on the eyelid can be flushed, then lifted off with a clean cotton swab; nothing touches the coloured part of the eye (MedlinePlus eye).
- An iron or steel fleck stuck on the clear front of the eye starts forming a rust ring after about 4 to 6 hours, and one left in can get pushed deeper (EyeWiki corneal). Clinics remove these at a slit lamp, under magnification (EyeWiki corneal), so get to a clinic, nurse or doctor the same day. Don't pick at the clear front of the eye with a needle, swab or corner of a cloth: EyeWiki describes removal as office or emergency-room work, done at an angle that avoids perforating the cornea (EyeWiki corneal).
- A fragment can go right into the eye with little pain and only a tiny entry mark, and the listed risk factors are metal-on-metal work and no eye protection (EyeWiki IOFB). If you felt something hit the eye while striking steel, treat it as possibly inside even if it hurts little and your sight seems fine: a fragment can go in without pain (EyeWiki IOFB). Don't try to remove it and don't press on the eye. Put a shield over it, not a pad: a clean paper cup taped on so it doesn't touch the eye, and loosely cover both eyes (MedlinePlus eye, EyeWiki IOFB, CRC First Aid).
- Infection is reported in 2 to 48 % of intraocular foreign body cases, and iron left in the eye can damage it over time (siderosis) (EyeWiki IOFB). This is one injury worth a long journey for.

### Steel splinter in the skin
- A sliver you can see: wash your hands, grip it with tweezers and pull it out at the angle it went in. If one end is just under the skin, sterilise a needle in rubbing alcohol or a flame and lift that end out (MedlinePlus splinter). Don't dig for a piece you can't see or that sits deep. Wash with soap and water, pat dry, and cover it if it will get dirty (MedlinePlus splinter).
- A deep or embedded piece: leave it in place, pad round it so it can't move, and bandage without pressing on it (CRC First Aid, [flying fragments](#browse/hazards/projectile)).
- Watch for infection over the next days: more redness, swelling, heat, pus, red streaks or fever ([sharp](#browse/hazards/sharp), [wound care](#ref/reference_first_aid/wounds)). A puncture from steel is a tetanus-prone wound: if the last tetanus shot was 5 or more years ago, get a booster when any clinic or nurse is reachable (CDC tetanus).
